name: Russet
lede: Russet is a dark, slightly orange brown, named for a coarse woollen cloth worn by the poor; across the centuries its meaning swung between honest poverty and the color of traitors.

sections.title: A cloth before a color
sections.body:
The word *russet* named a coarse woollen cloth before it named a color [1][9]. Paterson traces the color to that common cloth, and warns that the "russet yeas" in Shakespeare's *Love's Labour's Lost* have nothing to do with hue: the phrase means simple or homespun [9].

Because it was a cloth, russet never had a fixed color. The wool was dipped in weak baths of woad and then [[irresistible]], left over from dyeing the clothes of people higher up the social scale [1]. What came out depended on the dyes and on the natural shade of the fleece, and could be anything from dun through brown to grey [1]. To the medieval mind, St Clair explains, the closer a cloth stayed to its raw material, the cheaper and meaner it was [1].

sections.title: Cloth for carters
sections.body:
The best-known law is an English statute of 1363, in the thirty-seventh year of Edward III [1]. After dealing with lords, knights, clergy and merchants, it turned to carters, ploughmen, oxherds, cowherds, shepherds, threshers and everyone else with less than forty shillings in goods, and allowed them nothing but blanket and russet at twelvepence [1]. It was one case of a wider habit: from the mid-twelfth century, European sumptuary laws tied color to rank, confining dull earthy russet to the poorest rural people and leaving saturated [[scarlet]] to a select few [2]. St Clair reads the same pattern in dress at large: bright, colorfast dyes were costly, so brown was left to the poor [3].

Quality was another matter. Surviving records from the cloth market at Blackwell show a great deal of defective material, and Kentish russets, with 25 entries, were ranked behind only Gloucester whites (50) and Wiltshire goods (41) for poor workmanship [1]. On 13 April 1562 three people from Tonbridge and Benenden were fined for inferior russets, and one of them, William Watts, had been fined for the same fault the previous November [1].

sections.title: From the byword of the poor to plain honesty
sections.body:
Russet's symbolism moved as its color did. After the social upheaval of the Black Death, St Clair writes, it gradually came to stand for honesty, humility and manliness [1]. In *Piers Plowman*, the fourteenth-century allegory by William Langland, charity is as glad of a gown of grey russet as of a silk tunicle [1].

The double meaning was still alive in the Civil War [1]. In the autumn of 1643 Oliver Cromwell wrote that he would rather have a "plain russet-coated captain" who knew what he fought for than a gentleman who was nothing else [1]. Among the russet-heaviest pictures in our archive is [[painting:rijks-20028706|a Rijksmuseum portrait of Cromwell]] in a frame of allegorical figures, dated about 1650 [15]. The match says only that the color is there, not what the sitter wore [15].

sections.title: Russet, the color of traitors
sections.body:
A second russet ran in parallel, and it was not kind. Pastoureau describes a shade, which today we would call dark orange, that lost status from the twelfth century and gradually came to embody a whole list of vices [4]. The figure who came to personify it was Judas [4].

No New Testament or apocryphal text describes the apostle's appearance [4]. His red hair and beard appear only after the year 1000, first in miniatures, apparently in the lands of the Rhine and Meuse, and from the mid-thirteenth century they are almost always present [4]. Red hair was also given to Cain, to Reynard the fox and to other traitors and criminals [4].

The color word followed the hair. Pastoureau notes that *roux*, russet, seemed to combine the worst of red with the worst of yellow, and that tanné, a brownish red or dark russet, appears in sixteenth-century texts as the ugliest of all colors [5]. In medieval literature yellow and its superlative, russet, were tied to lying, trickery and hypocrisy, and the fox Renart's career as a false dyer is the standard example [8]. In the knightly romances a russet knight is a treacherous, hypocritical one [6].

Orange, which was not yet a separate color in medieval theory, was often confused with this despised russet, and began to detach itself from it only in the late Middle Ages, when the sweet orange from East Asia helped to raise its standing [7]. Pastoureau's own account is cautious about why [7].

sections.title: Two russets, one word
sections.body:
The two stories look contradictory: russet as the honest gown of the poor and russet as the mark of the liar. They are not the same russet. St Clair's evidence is English cloth, a brown or grey fabric, and its later praise [1]. Pastoureau's is the French and Latin *roux* and *rufus*, a reddish-yellow of hair and beards [4][7]. English had one word for both, and the color it named was unstable enough to carry them.

Ball makes the general point about such middle-ground words: when does puce become russet, burgundy or rust-red? He calls the answer partly a matter for perceptual psychology, and partly a window on how a language divides the world [13]. Even Van Gogh reached for the word, describing a shore as a sort of violet and faint russet, in a letter Ball quotes in his chapter on the painter [13].

sections.title: Field's russet
sections.body:
Painters met a third russet in the nineteenth century. George Field, the influential English colourman of the early 1800s, sold a transparent pigment called Field's russet, which the chemist Salter in 1869 described as a deep crimson-russet tinged with orange, halfway between orange and purple [11]. Salter gives it as a synonym of Rubens' madder and says it was made from madder [11]. Field himself, in 1835, mentions a madder brown that may be the same thing, a gently calcined madder lake [11].

Field also made tertiary pigments he called citrine, russet and olive [12]. His pure, transparent colors let the Pre-Raphaelites glaze thinly over white grounds around 1850 [12]. The painter's russet was thus a warm, glowing madder, nothing like the dull cloth, and the pigment names on a chart show the cloth word moving into the studio. A related English name appears in the entry for burnt ochre, where Field and Heaton call light red an ochre of orange russet hue, made by roasting Oxford ochre [11]. Related earths are [[sienna]] and [[burnt-umber]].

sections.title: The swatch and the season
sections.body:
Today most people hear autumn in the word. Paterson defines it as a shade of reddish brown, the colour of autumn, and lists russets with oranges, browns, yellows and reds among the colors of English leaves [9][10]. St Clair points out that this is recent: in Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930, russet was more orange than red-brown, with strong ashy grey undertones [1].

The swatch on this page is the modern reading. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 places it in block 55, "strong brown", within a ΔE of 2.6 [14]. A survey of screen users (xkcd) puts the word at a redder #A13905, so the name covers a wide patch of the brown-orange region [14]. Nearest on our chart is [[chocolate]], at a ΔE of 4.0, with [[saddle-brown]], [[tawny]], [[auburn]] and [[rust]] close by [14]. The same dictionary of 1930 also lists a *Russet Green*, a dull yellow-green recorded from 1731, so even the dictionary applied the word to more than brown [14].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Russet is a common painted color. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,683 works, or 7.1 per cent [15]. The share is highest in the 1420s, where 10 of 46 paintings qualify (21.7 per cent, three times the archive rate), and in the 1400s as a century (11.7 per cent) [15]. It falls to 6.2 per cent in the 1800s and 2.3 per cent in the 1900s, and only 3 of 140 Impressionist paintings in the archive qualify [15]. Among painters, 22 of George Dawe's 50 paintings carry it [15].

The leaders by share are not European at all: the largest share, 67 per cent of the canvas, is a Tibetan lineage painting in the Art Institute of Chicago, and Persian and Indian manuscript pages follow [15]. In the Western archive, russet usually fills the middle of the picture rather than its lights or darks: 67 per cent of its pixels in qualifying paintings sit in the mid-tones [15]. The colors it keeps company with are [[brown]], [[chocolate]], ochre and [[rust]] [15]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color and not a pigment test [15].

In Google Books, *russet* is already common in 1800, peaks around 1849 and by 2000 has fallen to about a fifth of that peak [16]. It is a word that peaked with the cloth it once named, and has been shrinking since.

questions.q: What did the word russet name before it was a color?
In 1363 English law told carters and ploughmen with little property to wear what?
Why did russet come to stand for honesty in some medieval and later English writing?
choices: It was the plain cloth of the poor, and after the Black Death that plainness read as humility
It was the color of royal robes
It was the only color the church allowed
It never faded in the sun
questions.answer: It was the plain cloth of the poor, and after the Black Death that plainness read as humility

openers: Russet was a cloth first: in 1363 English law told carters and ploughmen to wear blanket and russet.
In medieval art Judas gained red hair after the year 1000, and the russet word carried the stain.
